Thinking about this as the person who has to draw the actual screens and trace every path a visitor can take through them, here's where I land.

The one-sentence promise I'd commit to: this is a page where one specific couple pitches their future child's name up for playful "purchase" — visitors browse a sorted list of who's offered what, throw in their own name-and-amount pitch through a fake-charge checkout, and everyone understands from the headline down that the parents pick whatever they want regardless of dollar amount. That's the whole app. It should read like a wedding registry crossed with a Kickstarter backer list, not like an auction house.

Primary user is the offer-maker, not the parents. The parents are really just the seed content — there's no login, no owner dashboard, no "you have been outbid" notification loop, because building real auth and a notification system is exactly the kind of scope creep that turns a tight novelty page into a half-built platform. I want to state that decisively now rather than let it drift in later: no accounts anywhere in this build, for either the seed listing or a hypothetical second listing. The scenario is someone getting a link, reading the pitch in one glance, and either lurking or submitting a name + an amount + maybe a one-line story, going through a clearly-fake checkout, and seeing their entry land in the list.

The core loop I'd design around: land on hero (headline carries the joke and the disclaimer at once) → scroll to the sorted offer list → tap "make an offer" → fill name/alias/amount/optional story → hit a lightweight content filter → see the non-binding disclaimer directly in the submission flow, not just once somewhere upstream → go through the demo checkout (fake card, clearly labeled "no real charge") → get a confirmation only after the offer is actually persisted → see it appear in the sorted list. That loop needs to survive a visitor doing it twice in a row (repeat joke offers from the same person, no account to stop them) — I don't think we should block that, but I do think we need some soft rate-limit or the leaderboard turns into one person's name spammed ten times at the top.

Two structural things I don't think prior phases pinned down, and I think this phase is exactly where they should get pinned down instead of discovered mid-build. First: what does "sorted" mean when two offers tie on amount, and does the list ever close? The prompt implies an ongoing pitch with no end date, so I'd resolve it now as: sort by amount descending, tiebreak by earliest submission, status field exists but for MVP only ever reads "open" — there's no decision/close/winner-announcement flow, because that would require the parents to actually interact with the app, and there's no owner-facing surface for that. If that's wrong, it needs to be said explicitly as a cut, same as the marketplace. Second: report/flag says "confirms when used" but nobody defined what happens after that confirmation with no moderator logged in anywhere. I'd design it as self-moderating — a report is instant client-facing confirmation, and an item that crosses a small report threshold (say three) auto-hides from the public list without needing a human to review it. That's the only way "every listing and offer has a report control" is actually load-bearing rather than cosmetic, given there's no admin surface in scope.

On the marketplace: I'm going to just say it — cut it, and say so plainly in this phase's output rather than deferring again. It's been flagged as likely-cut twice already, the phase rules explicitly want ambiguity resolved decisively here, and every additional screen (create-listing form, browse/discovery page, per-listing routing) multiplies the states we have to get right in light/dark/mobile/desktop with zero payoff for the actual visitor persona we just defined. My biggest worry about my own position is that it does directly abandon half of what the user typed — but a marketplace nobody can discover anything in (no search, no categories, presumably just a flat list of strangers' pages) isn't really "a platform," it's a second half-finished feature bolted onto the thing that matters. If there's real appetite for it later, it's a clean v2, not a corner to cut on v1.

Success criteria I'd hold this to: a new visitor can state what the page is and what they can do without scrolling past the hero; a submission — content filter, disclaimer, fake checkout, persistence, confirmation, reappearance in the list — completes with zero dead ends on a phone; the offers list survives adversarial input (a 40-character alias, a $9,999,999 offer, three offers with identical amounts) without any text colliding in light or dark mode; and a zero-offer listing shows a real designed empty state that still explains the mechanic, not a blank list waiting for its first entry.
